Probing LLMs for Syntactic Structure Beyond Universal Dependencies: A Minimalist Phase Account in English

Yuanhao Chen     Peter Chin
Abstract

We show that LLMs encode syntactic distinctions not present in the Universal Dependencies (UD) tree distances that structural probes are trained to recover. On English wh-movement stimuli, we measure the probe distance between an embedded subject and its verb, whose UD tree distance is invariant across conditions. That distance is shorter than baseline when the embedded clause is finite and longer when it is infinitival — a within-clause sign asymmetry present in all 13 models across four families we test, at a majority of layers. No account based on UD distance, linear order, or monotone structural complexity can produce a sign reversal, while Minimalist phase theory can. Holding the matrix verb fixed while varying only the complement type reproduces the same finite–infinitival ordering in every model, ruling out a lexical-semantic explanation. The cross-clause pair separately reproduces the phase-count ordering of earlier work, validating the probes. A single activation patch, interchanging the clause-selecting matrix verb, moves the two pairs in opposite directions in 8 of 13 models. Because the causal intervention leaves the target string unchanged, it also rules out the clause-length and surface-cue explanations. Together these results reveal syntactic structure in LLMs beyond the UD probe target, and a Minimalist phase account is consistent with it.

1 Introduction

Structural probing has established that large language models (LLMs) encode syntactic structure in their hidden representations (Hewitt and Manning 2019; Manning et al. 2020). These probes train on Universal Dependencies (UD) tree distances as a consistent, broadly applicable annotation standard (de Marneffe et al. 2021), but explicitly not a generative grammar. Neural language models have become a testbed for formal linguistic theory, from early recurrent models (Marvin and Linzen 2018; Wilcox et al. 2018) to transformers (Kennedy 2025a; Kennedy 2025b). This raises a question that UD-like parsing cannot answer by construction: Do LLMs encode formal-syntactic abstractions (phase boundaries, phase-internal cohesion) that UD is not designed to represent?

We evaluate structural probes on English wh-movement stimuli constructed and verified per item so that UD-tree distances between the probed word pairs are invariant across conditions (Section 3.1). The three conditions — a bare small clause (an embedded subject and bare verb, with no embedded tense or complementiser), an infinitival, and a finite complement — are ordered by the number of Minimalist Program (MP) phase boundaries the wh-element crosses. The design follows Kennedy (2025a); Kennedy (2025b), who use UD-invariant complement-size contrasts to probe hierarchical structure: With UD distance held fixed, any condition effect must reflect structure beyond the UD distance.

Our central result is a within-clause sign asymmetry. The structural-probe distance between an embedded subject and the embedded verb reverses sign across conditions: smaller than the bare baseline in the finite condition, larger in the infinitival condition. No surface property predicts this. UD distance between the two words is invariant across conditions; linear word distance predicts no finite effect (the two tokens are adjacent in both bare and finite); and a monotone structural-complexity account predicts larger distances in both non-baseline conditions. The pattern is instead predicted by phase-internal cohesion — an MP abstraction invisible to the UD probe target by construction (Section 4.2). We make three contributions.

  1. 1.

    A within-clause sign asymmetry beyond UD (Section 4.2). On a probe pair whose UD distance is invariant across conditions, we find βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0 and βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0 (writing β\beta for a condition’s change in probe distance from the bare baseline), each at a majority of layers, in all 13 LLMs from four families. A same-verb control, holding the matrix verb fixed while varying only complement type, reproduces this ordering in all 13 models and rules out a lexical-semantic explanation. The reversal is predicted by MP phase-internal cohesion and is invisible to the UD tree-distance target by construction.

  2. 2.

    Opposite-signed causal effects (Section 4.3). A single activation patch, interchanging the clause-selecting matrix verb, shifts the cross-clause and within-clause probe pairs in opposite directions. Because the causal intervention leaves the target string unchanged, it removes the confounds an observational contrast cannot: It shows the within-clause asymmetry tracks phase status, not clause length, subject–verb agreement, or the intervening to.

  3. 3.

    A validated cross-clause ordering across a broad panel (Section 4.1). We reproduce and extend the cross-clause phase-count ordering of Kennedy (2025b) — the finite complement yields the largest wh-esubj separation, with βfin>0\beta_{\text{fin}}>0 and βfin>βinf\beta_{\text{fin}}>\beta_{\text{inf}} in all 13 models. Across four families and 1–27B parameters — a broader panel than the encoder-only setup of prior structural-probe work on generative syntax — both this ordering and the sign asymmetry hold, indicating the effects are not model-specific. The ordering also validates that our probes detect phase boundaries and supplies one of the two responses in the causal opposite-signed effect.

2 Background and Related Work

Phase theory.

Appendix B glosses syntactic terms used throughout. We treat clause structure in the framework of phase theory (Chomsky 2000; Chomsky 2001). A phase is a syntactic domain whose complement domain becomes inaccessible to higher derivational operations once the phase is complete. The two phase heads in English are v0, the light-verb head projecting a vP, and C, the head of CP. The wh-element crosses the matrix vP in every condition; a finite embedded clause adds two further phases along its path (the embedded vP and CP), an infinitival adds one (the embedded vP), and a bare small-clause complement adds none. Its movement path therefore spans three phase boundaries with a finite complement, two with an infinitival, and one with a bare complement.

We adopt the traditional analysis on which a bare perception or causative complement is a small clause projecting only a lexical VP and its subject (Stowell 1981), and so introduces no embedded phase; whether such complements instead project an eventive vP (hence a phase) is debated (Felser 1999), but the finite-versus-infinitival ordering that drives our central asymmetry (finite tighter than infinitival on esubj-evb) compares the two non-bare conditions and is unaffected by the bare baseline’s exact phase status.

The Phase Impenetrability Condition (PIC) restricts cross-phase operations to material at the phase edge (Chomsky 2001), forcing successive-cyclic wh-movement to transit each phase edge (van Urk 2020). Two predictions from this framework motivate our experimental design. The number of phase boundaries between the wh-position (matrix Spec,CP, after movement) and the base-position wh-copy at the embedded verb’s complement tracks the complement type: bare << infinitival << finite (Section 3.1). Arguments inside the same phase are structurally more cohesive than arguments separated by a phase boundary, even when their dependency-tree distance is identical (Section 4.2). The first motivates the cross-clause wh-esubj probe pair; the second motivates the within-clause esubj-evb pair (Section 3.1).

Phase-internal cohesion.

Beyond restricting cross-phase operations, phases are standardly taken to be the units of cyclic spell-out (Uriagereka 1999; Fox and Pesetsky 2005) and the domains within which agreement, case, and binding are computed (Bošković 2007; Lee-Schoenfeld 2008); sentence-processing work likewise finds integrative computation consolidating within-clause material at clause boundaries (Rayner, Kambe, and Duffy 2000). None of this is a representational claim about LLMs, but each gives a converging reason to expect items inside one completed phase to be represented more cohesively than items split across a phase boundary — the hypothesis we call phase-internal cohesion and test in Section 4.2.

Structural probes and prior evaluations.

A structural probe is a linear map from a model’s contextualised hidden states to a Euclidean space, trained so that pairwise distances approximate gold tree distances between words (Hewitt and Manning 2019; Manning et al. 2020); because training and evaluation both operate in UD, structural probing is by construction sensitive only to UD-grounded distinctions. Because an expressive probe can achieve high accuracy by fitting the mapping itself rather than reading structure off the representation, probe selectivity is a standard concern (Hewitt and Liang 2019); our design addresses it by holding the UD target invariant across conditions, so any condition effect must originate in the representation rather than in the probe’s UD-fitting capacity.

Kennedy (2025a); Kennedy (2025b) are the closest precedent: They evaluate structural probes on generative-syntax contrasts (subject raising vs. control; complement size) chosen so that UD does not directly encode the distinction. We share their design of holding UD distance invariant across conditions (verified per item, Section 3.1), but our contribution differs in kind: a within-clause sign asymmetry, a phase-internal-cohesion account of it, and a causal test. Their evidence also rests on a few small models (BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT-2, plus two sub-2B Qwen-2.5 models), whereas we test the phenomenon on 13 decoder-only LLMs of 1–27B parameters from four contemporary families — the autoregressive generation now in widespread use.

A parallel behavioural tradition assesses syntactic knowledge from model predictions, via minimal-pair acceptability (Marvin and Linzen 2018) or surprisal on controlled items (Wilcox et al. 2018; Koo and Kim 2026); Agarwal et al. (2025) show across 32 models that structural-probe accuracy does not predict minimal-pair performance, indicating that representational and behavioural methods recover different aspects of syntactic knowledge.

Whether a probed representation is causally active — whether intervening on it changes downstream representations, in the causal-abstraction sense (Geiger et al. 2023) — is distinct from whether the model’s behaviour relies on it; we test the former by activation patching (replacing an internal representation with one from a counterfactual input and measuring the downstream change, Section 4.3) and leave the latter open.

Effect size.

Our probes are trained on the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank (UD-EWT) (Silveira et al. 2014) with undirected dependency-tree distance as the gold target, then evaluated on our wh-movement stimuli without further fitting. We report an effect size β\beta: the estimated condition-vs.-bare difference in probe distance for a designated word pair (Section 3.2). Because our stimuli are constructed so that UD-tree distance between probed word pairs is invariant across conditions, verified per item (Section 3.1), a non-zero β\beta cannot be a re-encoding of the probe’s training target; it must reflect structural information that the UD tree distance does not encode.

3 Stimuli and Methods11 1 Code and stimuli: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/syntax-probe-147D.

3.1 Stimuli

Each item is a triple of wh-questions sharing the wh-element (what), the embedded-subject, and the embedded-verb, with the matrix verb and complement type varying by condition:

\ex

. [̇Bare: ] What did she see him eat? .̱[Infinitival: ] What did she expect him to eat? .̧[Finite: ] What did she think he ate?

The matrix verb is drawn from a condition-specific class. The bare matrix verb is a perception or causative verb (see, watch, make, let) selecting a bare small-clause complement (Stowell 1981). The infinitival matrix is an exceptional case-marking (ECM) or object-control verb (expect, want, allow, need) selecting an infinitival TP complement (Chomsky 1986).22 2 We use embedded subject for the accusative pronoun that is the logical subject of the embedded verb. Syntactically it is the embedded subject under ECM (expect) and the matrix object controlling a null PRO subject under object control (want, allow, need); the phase-cohesion mechanism of Section 4.2 is stated for the ECM case. The two subclasses yield comparable βinf\beta_{\text{inf}}, positive in all 13 models (Appendix G), so we treat the infinitival as a single class. On a raising-to-object analysis the pronoun attaches to the matrix verb, enlarging the within-clause distance; the design relies only on that distance being invariant across conditions, which we verify per item, not on its absolute value. The finite matrix is a bridge verb (think, believe, claim, say, know, suppose, report) selecting a finite CP complement with a null complementiser (Erteschik-Shir 1973). In the bare and infinitival conditions the embedded subject bears accusative case and the embedded verb appears in its base form; in the finite condition the embedded subject bears nominative case and the embedded verb appears in the simple past.

The three conditions are ordered by the number of phase boundaries crossed along the wh-movement path (Chomsky 2000; Chomsky 2001, Fig. 1;): bare small clause << infinitival TP << finite CP. We treat bare as the structural baseline: A contrast against bare measures the representational consequences of the additional clause structure.

We tag three positions per stimulus (what, embedded subject, embedded verb) and measure two probe distances: wh-esubj (what to embedded subject), capturing cross-clause structural depth as a function of complement type; and esubj-evb (embedded subject to embedded verb), capturing within-clause cohesion.

UD-distance invariance.

For probe-distance differences to be interpretable, the UD-tree distance between each probe pair must be constant across conditions within each item; otherwise differences in β\beta would be confounded with UD-level differences. We construct the stimuli from templates whose intended UD parse gives esubj-evb a single nsubj edge and wh-esubj a two-edge path, and we verify per item that the automatic parser keeps each distance constant across conditions. Parsing all 3,0003{,}000 stimuli with spaCy’s en_core_web_trf model (Honnibal et al. 2020, RoBERTa-based;) confirms the design — esubj-evb is fully invariant for 98.8%98.8\% of items (99.7%99.7\% in the same-verb control), and no item exceeds a one-edge spread. The residual one-edge spread falls on the wh-pairs, where the parser assigns a shorter infinitival path than finite; because this shortens rather than lengthens the infinitival distance, it runs against the predicted direction of the cross-clause effect and cannot inflate the false-positive rate. The check is scheme-independent — spaCy’s native Stanford-style scheme coincides with UD on the nsubj, direct-object, and clausal-complement edges that fix our pair distances, differing only in constructions absent from our stimuli (Appendix D gives per-pair rates, the parse figure, and the lexicon). Since our prediction is that probe distance increases with structural depth, this directional mismatch cannot manufacture the predicted effect.

Worked example: what each condition predicts.

The two probe pairs yield two independent, phase-based predictions across the three conditions (Fig. 1). For the wh-esubj pair, the wh-element transits every phase boundary on its movement path, so more boundaries mean greater representational separation: bare (11) << infinitival (22) << finite (33), predicting βfin>βinf>0\beta_{\text{fin}}>\beta_{\text{inf}}>0. For the esubj-evb pair, they are separated by a phase edge in both the infinitival and finite conditions, loosening it (βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0). But only in the finite condition, they share an extra phase (lower CP), and phase cohesion compensates in the other direction (βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0). The two pairs therefore carry opposite finite-condition signs, the contrast the causal experiment later exploits (Section 4.3).

Lexicon and item generation.

The combinatorial lexicon comprises 77 matrix subjects, 77 embedded subjects (in matched accusative/nominative pairs), 44 bare-class matrix verbs, 44 infinitival-class verbs, 77 bridge verbs, and 2020 embedded transitive verbs with inanimate-compatible objects. Items are constrained so that the matrix and embedded subjects differ and so that the three matrix verbs are mutually distinct within an item. The combination yields on the order of 10510^{5} candidate items; we use a fixed seed-controlled sample of 1,0001{,}000 items, yielding 3,0003{,}000 stimuli (one per condition per item).

3.2 Probing Setup

Probe training.

We follow the structural-probe protocol of Hewitt and Manning (2019). For each transformer layer ℓ\ell, we obtain a per-word representation hw(ℓ)∈ℝdh_{w}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} by mean-pooling the subword-token hidden states at layer ℓ\ell for each word ww (dd is the model’s hidden size). We then train a linear projection B(ℓ)∈ℝr×dB^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} with r=64r=64, defining the probe distance between any two words u,vu,v at layer ℓ\ell as

dB(ℓ)​(u,v)≔∥B(ℓ)​(hu(ℓ)−hv(ℓ))∥22,d_{B}^{(\ell)}(u,v)\;\coloneqq\;\big\lVert B^{(\ell)}\big(h_{u}^{(\ell)}-h_{v}^{(\ell)}\big)\big\rVert_{2}^{2},

the squared L2 norm of the projected difference (Hewitt and Manning 2019, eq. 1). B(ℓ)B^{(\ell)} is fit by minimising L1 loss between dB(ℓ)​(u,v)d_{B}^{(\ell)}(u,v) and the gold undirected dependency-tree distance between u,vu,v on the UD-EWT training corpus (Silveira et al. 2014), using Adam (learning rate 10−310^{-3}, batch size 256256) for up to 100100 epochs with learning-rate decay on plateau (factor 0.10.1, patience 11, up to 44 resets). Input activations are standardised per training corpus before projection. The resulting per-layer probes are then evaluated on our wh-movement stimuli without further fitting.

Effect-size estimation.

For each (model, layer ℓ\ell, pair) we fit one treatment-coded ordinary least squares (OLS) regression

di,k(ℓ)=\displaystyle d^{(\ell)}_{i,k}\;=\;\; β0(ℓ)+βfin(ℓ)⋅𝟙{ci,k=fin}\displaystyle\beta_{0}^{(\ell)}+\beta_{\text{fin}}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathds{1}\{c_{i,k}=\text{fin}\}
+βinf(ℓ)⋅𝟙{ci,k=inf}+εi,k(ℓ),\displaystyle\phantom{\beta_{0}^{(\ell)}}+\beta_{\text{inf}}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathds{1}\{c_{i,k}=\text{inf}\}+\varepsilon^{(\ell)}_{i,k},

where di,k(ℓ)d^{(\ell)}_{i,k} is the probe distance dB(ℓ)d_{B}^{(\ell)} for the relevant word pair in stimulus kk of item ii, ci,kc_{i,k} is the condition, 𝟙​{⋅}\mathds{1}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function, εi,k(ℓ)\varepsilon^{(\ell)}_{i,k} is the error term, and bare is the reference category (so β0(ℓ)\beta_{0}^{(\ell)} is the bare-condition mean probe distance). Empirically β0\beta_{0} is on the order of 2–3 across models and layers, so the condition effects β\beta we report (roughly 0.10.1–0.50.5) are modest fractions of that baseline (about 5–20%). The primary coefficients are the contrast slopes βfin(ℓ)\beta_{\text{fin}}^{(\ell)} (finite −- bare) and βinf(ℓ)\beta_{\text{inf}}^{(\ell)} (infinitival −- bare). The three conditions of an item share lexical content, so we fit the regression with cluster-robust (CR1) standard errors clustered on the item (1,0001{,}000 clusters), rather than treating the 3,0003{,}000 stimuli as independent. We apply Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995) across all (layer ×\times pair ×\times contrast) tests within each model.

3.3 Layer Reporting

Structural-probing effects vary across layers, and reporting only a per-model peak βpeak=maxℓ⁡β(ℓ)\beta^{\text{peak}}=\max_{\ell}\beta^{(\ell)} (Hewitt and Manning 2019; Manning et al. 2020) is opportunistic, especially when different contrasts peak at different layers (in our panel, 00 of 1313 models share a peak layer for βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} and βinf\beta_{\text{inf}} on wh-esubj). We therefore report each effect breadth-first: the fraction of layers at which it holds in the predicted direction under FDR correction, a summary that privileges no single layer.

When a per-pair anchor is needed to site the causal intervention’s measurement (Section 4.3), we use the reference layer: L∗≔arg⁡maxℓ⁡βfin(ℓ)L^{\ast}\coloneqq\operatorname*{\arg\max}_{\ell}\beta_{\text{fin}}^{(\ell)} for the cross-clause pair, and arg⁡maxℓ⁡(βinf(ℓ)−βfin(ℓ))\operatorname*{\arg\max}_{\ell}(\beta_{\text{inf}}^{(\ell)}-\beta_{\text{fin}}^{(\ell)}) for the within-clause pair — in each case the layer at which that pair’s effect is strongest. The causal intervention reads Δ​β\Delta\beta (the change in a pair’s contrast induced by activation patching) within the reference band L∗±1L^{\ast}\pm 1 (the reference layer and its immediate neighbours, floored at layer 3 so the patch site stays strictly upstream), with L∗L^{\ast} fixed by the observational effect β\beta, not by the causal effect Δ​β\Delta\beta.

The two effects call for different summaries. The observational effect is broad across layers, so we report the layer fraction above. The causal effect is instead layer-localised (concentrating near L∗L^{\ast}), so we report its dominant in-band value (the largest-magnitude significant Δ​β\Delta\beta in the band) rather than a layer fraction; at n=1,000n=1{,}000 a layer fraction would let a tiny opposite-signed blip one layer away, significant only at this sample size, weigh equally with the main effect. Significance of each in-band Δ​β\Delta\beta comes from a clustered bootstrap over items (n=1,000n=1{,}000 resamples, percentile 95%95\% confidence interval (CI)), with a Δ​β\Delta\beta significant when its CI excludes 00.

3.4 Models

We evaluate on 13 decoder-only language models from four families: Gemma-3 (Gemma Team et al. 2025), Llama-3 (Grattafiori et al. 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al. 2023), and Qwen (Qwen Team et al. 2025; Yang et al. 2025). All models are base (non-instruction-tuned) pretrained checkpoints, accessed via the HuggingFace Transformers library; the full panel is in Appendix A. Probe training and evaluation were run on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU; total wall-clock time was under two hours.

4 Experiments

4.1 Observational Validation: The Cross-Clause Phase-Count Ordering

We first confirm that our probes detect phase boundaries at all, on the cross-clause wh-esubj pair, replicating and extending Kennedy (2025b) across the panel. Estimating βfin(ℓ)\beta_{\text{fin}}^{(\ell)} and βinf(ℓ)\beta_{\text{inf}}^{(\ell)} at every layer and summarising each contrast breadth-first (Section 3.3), we find the finite condition yields the largest separation — βfin>0\beta_{\text{fin}}>0 and βfin>βinf\beta_{\text{fin}}>\beta_{\text{inf}} in all 13 models (Fig. 2, left) — so each added phase boundary between the wh-filler and the embedded subject increases their representational separation, most strongly for the finite complement. The finite–bare contrast is broad and reliable. The panel median of FDR-significant positive layers for βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} is 94%94\% (five of 13 models reach ≥97%\geq 97\%; lowest 63%63\%, Gemma-3-1B), with the median βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} across FDR-significant layers ranging from +0.10+0.10 (Gemma-3-1B) to +0.50+0.50 (Gemma-3-27B; Fig. 2, left). The smaller one-phase infinitival step βinf\beta_{\text{inf}} is weaker and more layer-localised: positive at a majority of FDR-significant layers in 10 of 13 models, with a panel-median marker near zero or slightly negative in the other three (Gemma-3-1B, Gemma-3-27B, and Qwen-3-8B; Fig. 2, left). This is expected, because the infinitival is the one condition whose wh-esubj UD distance is not strictly invariant. The parser assigns a shorter path in a minority of items, working against βinf\beta_{\text{inf}}, whereas the finite–bare invariance (both 22 edges) is stable and isolates a clean beyond-UD effect. The basis for βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0 is derivational: The phrase-structure distance from what to the embedded subject is equal in the bare and infinitival conditions, but the infinitival subject is base-merged at the phase edge (Spec,vP) while the bare subject is not (Appendix C; Chomsky 2001). This ordering is the observational counterpart of one of the two responses in the causal opposite-signed effect (Section 4.3); the novel result is the within-clause pair, which we focus on next.

4.2 Within-Clause Cohesion: The Sign Asymmetry

We turn from the cross-clause pair to the within-clause pair — the embedded subject and the embedded verb (esubj-evb) — whose UD-tree distance is invariant across conditions, a single nsubj edge in the intended parse (Fig. 1). Here we find a robust sign asymmetry: βfin<0<βinf\beta_{\text{fin}}<0<\beta_{\text{inf}}. Reported breadth-first (Section 3.3), every one of the 13 models, across all four families, shows βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0 and βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0 at a majority of layers (per-model values in Appendix F). Across the panel the median β\beta over FDR-significant layers is negative for βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} and positive for βinf\beta_{\text{inf}} in every model, with magnitudes of roughly 0.10.1–0.30.3 on each side (Fig. 2, right). Because the two contrasts have opposite predicted signs, a shared reference layer does not apply; the asymmetry is a property of the layer profile, not of any single layer.

Three observations rule out simpler accounts.

First, the UD distance between the two words is invariant across conditions (Fig. 1), so a pure UD-decoding probe would yield β≈0\beta\approx 0. Second, the linear distance between the two words is 11 in bare and finite but 22 in infinitival (the to marker intervenes). A surface-linear-distance heuristic predicts βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0 and βfin≈0\beta_{\text{fin}}\approx 0; the observed negative βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} cannot come from linear distance. Third, a monotone structural-complexity heuristic (more tree structure between the two words means larger probe distance) predicts βinf≳βfin≳0\beta_{\text{inf}}\gtrsim\beta_{\text{fin}}\gtrsim 0 (inequality or equality depending on simplified structure, Fig. 1, or full structure, Appendix C), with either interpretation yielding βfin≳0\beta_{\text{fin}}\gtrsim 0. The observed negative βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} directly contradicts these predictions.

One alternative these observations do not address is subject–verb agreement — the finite condition alone pairs a nominative subject with a tensed verb, so βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0 could reflect an agreement relation rather than phase-internal cohesion. The observational contrast cannot remove this confound; the causal test in Section 4.3 is designed to exclude it.

A same-verb control.

A further alternative is that the asymmetry reflects the lexical semantics of the matrix verb rather than clause structure: Our finite conditions use attitude verbs and our infinitival conditions expectation and desire verbs. To rule this out we ran a same-verb control that fixes the matrix verb at expect, which independently licenses both a finite complement (What did she expect he ate?) and an infinitival one (What did she expect him to eat?). It is the rare verb admitting both with matched aspect; epistemic alternatives such as believe require a perfect infinitival (“believe him to have eaten,” not “believe him to eat”), which would reintroduce an aspectual confound. A same-verb design admits no bare condition, since expect takes no bare complement, so only the finite–infinitival difference is strictly verb-matched; we therefore test the verb-matched contrast βinf−βfin\beta_{\text{inf}}-\beta_{\text{fin}}, which cancels the bare baseline. Holding the verb fixed, the infinitival condition yields a larger esubj-evb probe distance than the finite condition at a majority of layers in all 13 models (FDR-corrected; median βinf−βfin\beta_{\text{inf}}-\beta_{\text{fin}} between 0.190.19 and 0.390.39), reproducing the ordering above with matrix-verb identity and lexical semantics held constant (Appendix H).

From the PIC to representations.

The PIC (Chomsky 2000; Chomsky 2001) is a constraint on syntactic derivation. It determines which operations the grammar can perform across phase boundaries, and is not a claim about representational geometry in itself. To connect phase theory to the observed sign asymmetry we therefore need an additional assumption. The candidate is phase-internal cohesion: Items inside the same completed phase are spelled out as a unit and share locality-domain status, leading to more shared computation than structural depth alone predicts and making them representationally closer in the model’s hidden states (Section 2).

Why esubj-evb specifically.

Phase cohesion would in principle apply to any pair of items inside the same phase; its predictive force differs across our two probe pairs for a structural reason. For esubj-evb, both items lie inside the embedded clause, and the matrix phases contain them identically in every condition, cancelling against the bare baseline; only the embedded structure between and around them varies. In the bare condition they occupy a single minimal domain with no embedded phase separating them — the baseline. In the infinitival condition an embedded vP intervenes (the verb inside it, the subject above it) with no embedded CP containing both, so they straddle a phase edge and we observe βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0. In the finite condition the same embedded vP intervenes, but an embedded CP now contains both; the shared CP tightens the pair more than the vP loosens it, and we observe βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0 against the bare baseline. For wh-esubj, the two items span clause boundaries and are never co-internal to any embedded phase, so phase cohesion has no effect.

We treat phase cohesion as one possible account. The strong empirical claim is the sign asymmetry itself (βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0 and βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0 in all 13 models, each at a majority of layers) which no UD-, linear-, or monotone-complexity-based account predicts.

4.3 Opposite-Signed Causal Effects: The Matrix-Verb Interchange

The two observational signatures (Sections 4.1 and 4.2) are not causal. They show phase structure is encoded, not that it is used. A single activation patch tests both, and removes the one confound the observational within-clause result cannot.

The confound an observational contrast cannot exclude.

The esubj-evb asymmetry compares probe distances across strings that differ in surface form: The infinitival inserts to between the two probed words, lengthening the clause. An observational contrast therefore cannot fully separate phase structure from clause length, the intervening token, or the subject–verb agreement that co-varies with finiteness. The activation patch below leaves the target string unchanged (it edits only the model’s internal representation of the matrix verb), so the tokens whose probe distance we measure, their linear positions, and the embedded clause’s (non-)agreement are identical before and after. A non-zero effect thus cannot arise from any property of the target string itself (its length, token frequency, agreement, or surface form) since all are held fixed.

Design.

The matrix verb is the most immediate surface c-commander of both the embedded subject and the embedded verb (Fig. 1). For a matched item pair differing only in matrix-verb class, we run the model on the target sentence and replace the residual stream at the matrix-verb position with the corresponding representation from the source sentence, patching at the earliest layers where the injected feature can propagate furthest downstream.33 3 Both responses are strongest when patched at layer 1 and decay as the patch layer approaches the measurement layer. We then read Δ​β=βpatched−βtarget\Delta\beta=\beta_{\text{patched}}-\beta_{\text{target}} on both probe pairs, each measured in its own reference band (Section 3.3). The interchange is run in both directions — finite→\rightarrowinfinitival (inject a finite matrix verb into an infinitival target) and infinitival→\rightarrowfinite — and, as a control, within the same condition (finite↔\leftrightarrowfinite, infinitival↔\leftrightarrowinfinitival), which changes the matrix verb’s lexical identity but not the clause it selects.

Predictions.

If the probe pairs track phase structure, one manipulation should move them in opposite directions. Injecting a finite verb adds a phase boundary between wh and the embedded subject (pushing wh-esubj up) while placing the embedded subject and verb inside a shared embedded CP (pulling esubj-evb down); the infinitival direction mirrors both signs. A same-class swap also perturbs the representation, but with no consistent sign, whereas the between-class swap has the predicted opposite signs. The target retains its own surface cues (to, agreement) that compete with the injected signal, so a directional effect is strong evidence while a null is uninformative.

Results.

Figure 3 plots the dominant in-band Δ​β\Delta\beta on the two probe pairs for each model and interchange direction; Appendix I gives the underlying per-model values including controls. A response counts as confirmed when the sign of its dominant in-band Δ​β\Delta\beta is predicted; the effect is layer-localised (Section 3.3), so the predicted sign need not hold at every band layer. All four cells shift in the predicted direction in 8 of 13 models, and at least one interchange direction shows the opposite-signed shift in 11 of 13, with dominant |Δ​β||\Delta\beta| typically 0.20.2–0.60.6. Pair by pair, the cross-clause wh-esubj effect is confirmed in both directions in 11 of 13 models and the within-clause esubj-evb effect in 10 of 13; the within-class controls carry no consistent sign and are, per pair, smaller than the between-class effect they control. The failures are informative rather than noise. In Gemma-3-1B and Qwen-2.5-7B, the cross-clause response reverses in-band in both directions, while the within-clause response behaves as predicted. Gemma-3-27B, Qwen-3-1.7B, and Qwen-3-4B instead lose only the finite→\rightarrowinfinitival within-clause response; Qwen-3-4B shows a reversed within-clause effect there (Δ​β=+0.35\Delta\beta=+0.35 where the prediction is negative), suggesting its within-clause asymmetry is more surface- or length-driven than phase-driven, precisely the alternative this experiment is built to detect.

Interpretation.

On a monotone account, adding structure can only increase probe distances, so it cannot make one pair’s distance fall while the other’s rises. The opposite-signed effect therefore requires pair-specific structure, of the kind phase-internal cohesion describes. With the string held fixed, the same causal intervention which raises cross-clause separation also tightens phase-internal cohesion. This is the strongest evidence we have that both signatures reflect one causally active phase structure rather than two surface correlations.

5 Discussion

Structural encoding below the UD surface.

The esubj-evb sign asymmetry (βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0 and βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0 in all 13 models, each at a majority of layers) is our clearest demonstration that LLM representations carry structural information the UD probe target does not capture. No UD-distance, surface-linear, or monotone-complexity account predicts a sign reversal (Section 4.2); phase-internal cohesion does. A same-verb control, holding the matrix verb fixed, further excludes a lexical-semantic account. The finite tightening is also broad across the lexicon. Broken down by embedded verb, βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} is negative for all 20 verbs in 11 of 13 models, and for at least 18 of 20 in the other two, so it is not carried by a few frequent subject-verb bigrams. That it holds across four model families suggests distributional pretraining can induce representations aligned with formal-syntactic abstractions beyond the reach of annotation-based probing.

From correlation to one causal structure.

The matrix-verb interchange (Section 4.3) turns two correlations into one causally active structure. A single edit to the clause-selecting verb moves the cross-clause and within-clause pairs in opposite directions. This is the two-way pattern phase-internal cohesion predicts, and no monotone account of depth, length, or complexity can produce it. Because the edit leaves the target string fixed, it also closes the length-, agreement-, frequency-, and surface-cue loophole on the central asymmetry that an observational contrast must leave open. The causal intervention shows that phase information is causally active among the model’s representations, not merely correlated with them; whether the model’s behaviour relies on this structure — the sense at issue in Agarwal et al. (2025) — is a separate question we leave open.

Implications.

Commonly adopted UD-based parses provide merely a lower bound on syntactic encoding happening in LLMs. An invariant UD tree distance does not mean a distinction is absent from the representation, only that it is invisible to a probe trained on that distance. Substantively, that models trained only to predict tokens represent a phase-level organisation posited on independent linguistic grounds is a representational data point for the broader question of how far LLM internal structure aligns with generative syntax.

6 Limitations

Language.

All stimuli are in English. The predictions follow from phase structure, which generalises cross-linguistically, but the three-way complement-size contrast exploits English-specific verb classes and case morphology. Languages with overt morphological or word-order diagnostics for phase structure — V2 languages, where finite verbs move to C, or ergative languages with distinct case–phase interactions — would offer a more stringent test.

Model-level variability and scope.

The causal responses are not universal: The within-clause effect fails or reverses in the finite→\rightarrowinfinitival direction for three models and the observational βinf\beta_{\text{inf}} reverses in one, while the cross-clause response reverses in two further models (Sections 4.1 and 4.3). We have no principled account of why specific models depart. The panel is 13 publicly available base models (1–27B) from four families; instruction-tuned, mixture-of-experts, and larger models are untested.

Appendix B Syntactic Terminology

This appendix glosses the syntactic terms used throughout the paper.

We use standard X-bar notation, in which a head X projects an intermediate level X′ that combines X with its complement, and a maximal phrase XP; the specifier (Spec,XP) is the phrase’s structurally highest internal position. The projections relevant here are the CP (complementiser phrase, headed by C, whose specifier Spec,CP is the landing site for wh-movement), the TP (tense phrase, whose specifier hosts the surface subject), the vP (light-verb phrase, which introduces the external argument in Spec,vP), the VP (lexical-verb phrase, containing the verb and its complement), and the DP (determiner phrase, the maximal nominal projection covering subjects, objects, and wh-phrases). A node c-commands its sister and all its sister’s descendants.

A phase is a cyclic spell-out domain; in MP English the phase heads are the transitive light verb v and the complementiser C, so vP and CP are phases whereas TP and VP are not. Once a phase is complete, the Phase Impenetrability Condition (PIC) makes its complement inaccessible to operations outside the phase, leaving only the phase head and its edge (the specifier) available. Long-distance wh-movement must therefore be successive-cyclic, halting at each intervening phase edge — Spec,vP and Spec,CP — on its way to the matrix Spec,CP (Chomsky 2001).

Our stimuli turn on a small set of clause types. A small clause is a minimal complement of only a VP and its subject, lacking TP and vP, as in the bracketed portion of “she saw [him eat the cake]”. Under exceptional case-marking (ECM) the matrix verb assigns accusative case to the overt subject of an infinitival complement — him, not he, in “she expected him to leave”. A bridge verb such as think or say permits wh-extraction from its finite CP complement, and the long-distance relation between the fronted wh-phrase and its extraction site is a filler–gap dependency.

Appendix D Stimulus Lexicon and Verification

Lexicon.

The combinatorial lexicon of Section 3.1 has the following members. Matrix subjects: she, he, they, I, the teacher, the manager, the detective. Embedded subjects, as matched accusative/nominative pairs: him/he, her/she, us/we, them/they, and the student, the assistant, the suspect (identical in both cases). Bare small-clause verbs: see and watch (visual perception), make and let (causative); hear and have are excluded (an auditory selectional restriction and an auxiliary clash, respectively). Infinitival verbs: expect (ECM), and want, allow, need (object control). Finite bridge verbs: think, believe, claim, say, know, suppose, report. Embedded transitive verbs, each taking an inanimate-compatible object, with a mix of regular and irregular past forms: eat, buy, read, write, build, fix, find, clean, cook, sell, carry, paint, break, steal, bring, open, send, drop, use, take. Two constraints prune the Cartesian product: The matrix subject must differ from the embedded subject, and the three matrix verbs within an item must be distinct. The result is a pool of roughly 128,000128{,}000 valid items, from which a fixed seed-controlled shuffle takes the first 1,0001{,}000. An earlier version of the lexicon also listed convince and require as infinitival verbs; a scale check flagged both because spaCy attaches their post-verbal noun phrase as a direct object rather than an embedded subject, placing the probed pair two edges off the design in 3737 items, so they were removed and need was substituted.

Distances and verification.

The stimuli are templated so that each probed-pair distance is constant across conditions (Fig. 5), verified per item on the automatic parse (Table 2). To confirm this automatically, we parse all 3,0003{,}000 stimuli with spaCy en_core_web_trf, compute the UD tree distance from that parse for each probed pair in each condition, and record every item’s spread: the largest minus the smallest of its three condition distances. An item passes when its spread is at most one edge. Table 2 reports the fraction of items that are fully distance-invariant (spread 00), for the main experiment and the same-verb control (Appendix H). All 3,0003{,}000 stimuli parse in both experiments, and no item exceeds the one-edge tolerance.

Appendix E Probe Training Quality

All 13 probes show the standard structural-probe quality profile on the UD-EWT validation set (Fig. 6) — a rise from the embedding layer to a mid-network plateau, then a moderate decline near the output — with a peak distance Spearman correlation (predicted vs. gold tree distances) of 0.650.65–0.760.76 and UUAS of 0.560.56–0.670.67 across models, indicating substantial recovery of dependency structure. Our analysis does not otherwise hinge on absolute probe quality — the effect sizes β\beta are within-probe contrasts between conditions on the same probe, so a probe’s overall recovery level bounds neither their sign nor their significance.

Appendix F Per-Model Observational Effects

Table 3 gives the per-model within-clause esubj-evb effect behind Fig. 2, the numeric basis for the sign asymmetry. In every model the finite contrast is significantly negative and the infinitival contrast significantly positive at a majority of layers, so βfin<0\beta_{\text{fin}}<0 and βinf>0\beta_{\text{inf}}>0 each hold panel-wide.

Appendix G ECM versus Object-Control

The infinitival class combines one ECM verb (expect) and three object-control verbs (want, allow, need). Splitting the within-clause infinitival contrast βinf\beta_{\text{inf}} by subclass shows the two behave alike. βinf\beta_{\text{inf}} is positive in all 13 models for each subclass, of comparable magnitude (Table 4), which justifies pooling the infinitival verbs into a single class in the main text.

Appendix H Same-Verb Control (Lexically Matched)

Section 4.2 reports a same-verb control that holds the matrix verb fixed at expect across the finite and infinitival conditions, isolating complement structure from matrix-verb identity and lexical semantics. The stimuli reuse the main generator with the matrix verb locked to expect in both the finite condition (What did she expect he ate?) and the infinitival condition (What did she expect him to eat?); the bare condition keeps a small-clause verb (see, watch, make, let) as the baseline, since expect takes no bare complement. We apply the trained probes to these stimuli without retraining. Because the bare condition cannot share the matrix verb, only the finite–infinitival difference is strictly verb-matched, so we report the verb-matched contrast βinf−βfin\beta_{\text{inf}}-\beta_{\text{fin}}, which cancels the bare baseline. UD-distance invariance for the experimental pairs was verified on all 3,000 stimuli under the same criterion as the main stimuli (Section 3.1).

Table 5 gives per-model estimates. The verb-matched ordering βinf−βfin>0\beta_{\text{inf}}-\beta_{\text{fin}}>0 is FDR-significant with the predicted sign at a majority of layers in all 13 models, with median βinf−βfin\beta_{\text{inf}}-\beta_{\text{fin}} between 0.190.19 and 0.390.39. Against the cross-verb bare baseline βinf\beta_{\text{inf}} is positive in every model, while βfin\beta_{\text{fin}} has a model-dependent sign — expect is a less prototypical finite-complement verb than the bridge verbs of the main experiment, so its finite arm sits closer to the baseline — and the verb-matched difference, which combines both, is positive throughout. This control isolates matrix-verb semantics; it does not address clause length, which the causal interchange (Section 4.3) removes separately.

Appendix I Per-Model Interchange Effects

Table 6 gives the per-model coordinates behind Fig. 3: for each interchange direction and probe pair, the dominant in-band Δ​β\Delta\beta (Section 4.3). The opposite-signed prediction is that fin→\toinf raises wh-esubj and lowers esubj-evb, and inf→\tofin does the reverse. All four cells carry the predicted sign in 8 of 13 models, and at least one interchange direction moves both pairs in their predicted opposite directions in 11 of 13; the within-class controls, which swap the matrix verb for another of the same phase class, carry no consistent sign and are far smaller. Figure 7 profiles these effects across the reference band, showing they concentrate near L∗L^{*} rather than holding across it.
